summary: Surveys use of IPv4 addresses in IETF Transport Area standards-track and experimental documents, to find dependencies on IPv4. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist of delivery rules that mention old-style addresses, so they can be updated.

questions: ipv4 dependencies in transport area specs
subtitle: A catalog of IPv4 address dependencies in transport area standards.

tldr.problem: Transport layer protocols and mechanisms were designed when IPv4 was the only IP version, leaving some with dependencies that could hinder IPv6 transition.
tldr.mechanism: This document systematically surveys all standards-track and experimental RFCs in the Transport Area, identifying which contain IPv4-specific provisions. The Transport Area covers TCP, UDP, RTP, RSVP, and other protocols above the IP layer.
tldr.outcome: The survey identified 24 out of 104 RFCs with IPv4 dependencies, concentrated in older standards like TCP checksums, NetBIOS, and media description protocols that were already being updated.

today: RFC 3794 is Informational and documents the Transport Area's IPv6 readiness as of June 2004. Most identified issues have since been addressed: RFC 2460 updated TCP checksums for IPv6, RFCs 3266 and others extended session description protocols, and measurement protocols received IPv6 support. The document remains a historical reference showing how a major standards area successfully adapted to IPv6 transition.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This survey document examines IPv6 readiness in the Transport Area, which defines how applications send and receive data. The Transport Area covers foundational protocols like TCP and UDP, real-time protocols like RTP, quality-of-service mechanisms, and many others.

Unlike the IP layer itself, transport protocols often interact with addresses when they form checksums, carry routing information, or describe media sessions. This survey identifies which transport standards rely on IPv4-specific features that might require supplementary specifications or updates for full IPv6 support.
sections.plainLanguage: This document checks the middle layer of how computers talk to each other, to see which rules only work with old-style addresses.

sections.title: Scope and Methodology
sections.content:
The survey examined 104 transport-related RFCs: 5 Full Standards, 2 Draft Standards, 82 Proposed Standards, and 15 Experimental RFCs. Each was analyzed for IPv4-specific text, address fields, or protocol procedures that assume IPv4. The analysis spans transport protocols, session description, congestion control, real-time applications, and network measurement.

The survey identifies both critical dependencies (like TCP's checksum computation) and minor ones (like example IPv4 addresses in documentation). Some standards already had published IPv6 updates; others were being addressed by active working groups at the time of publication.
sections.plainLanguage: The document looks at 104 different transport rules, checking each for anything tied to old-style addresses.

sections.title: Key IPv4 Dependencies Identified
sections.content:
The survey found 24 out of 104 RFCs with IPv4 dependencies (23%). The breakdown was: 3 out of 5 Full Standards (60%), 0 out of 2 Draft Standards, 17 out of 82 Proposed Standards (21%), and 4 out of 15 Experimental RFCs (27%).

Critical dependencies include TCP's pseudo-header checksum (RFC 793), which uses source and destination IPv4 addresses, and NetBIOS over TCP/UDP (RFCs 1001 and 1002), which carries IPv4 addresses throughout its protocol. Less critical dependencies involve media description formats, routing metrics, and service specifications that assume IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: About one in four of the 104 rules have ties to old-style addresses. The most important ones are in older, widely-used protocols.

sections.title: Major Issues and Ongoing Work
sections.content:
The most significant issue is TCP checksums (RFC 793). TCP checksums cover a pseudo-header containing 32-bit source and destination IPv4 addresses. This is addressed in RFC 2460 (IPv6 Specification) with updated pseudo-header definitions for IPv6. NetBIOS (RFCs 1001, 1002) carries IPv4 addresses throughout its protocol and requires a complete new specification for IPv6 support.

Session description standards like SDP (RFC 2327) and RTSP (RFC 2326) initially used IPv4-only formats but were being updated—SDP received IPv6 support in RFC 3266, and RTSP was addressed through IPv6 literal address formats. Network measurement protocols (IPPM RFCs 2678-2681) were restricted to IPv4 but working groups were developing IPv6 versions. Other standards like RTP, compression protocols, and quality-of-service mechanisms either had no IPv4 dependencies or were already IPv6-aware.
sections.plainLanguage: Some older rules have real problems: TCP's checksum math uses IPv4 addresses, and NetBIOS is full of IPv4. But many groups were already working on fixes for these.

sections.title: Status and Resolutions
sections.content:
Many identified issues were already resolved or being addressed by the time of publication. TCP header compression (RFC 1144) was resolved by RFC 2508. RPC binding (RFC 1833) issues could be fixed by defining an IPv6 protocol family. ISO transport over TCP (RFC 1006) was updated in RFC 2126 with full IPv6 support. Working groups were actively addressing measurement protocols, SDP, and other standards.

Standards that had no IPv4 dependencies at all—such as congestion control algorithms, RTP profiles, and many security protocols—required no action. The survey confirms that while transport standards have more IPv4 dependencies than other areas, most are being addressed through a combination of supplements, updates, and working group activity.
sections.plainLanguage: Many problems were already being fixed. Rules that don't care about addresses are fine as-is. The ones that do care are getting updated.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 3794 is an Informational document that documented the Transport Area's IPv6 readiness in 2004. Since then, most identified issues have been resolved: TCP now has IPv6 checksum definitions, session description protocols support IPv6, and measurement protocols have been extended. The document remains a valuable historical reference for understanding how fundamental transport standards adapted to IPv6.

For operators deploying IPv6, this document identifies which transport standards might require attention or supplementary specifications. Most modern operating systems and applications now support both IPv4 and IPv6 at the transport layer, fulfilling the promise outlined in this survey.
sections.plainLanguage: This document proved that transport standards could be updated for new addresses. Most fixes are now done, and new rules are being written to support both types of addresses.
